title: A Survey for Deep Reinforcement Learning Based Network Intrusion Detection
document_text: A Survey for Deep Reinforcement Learning Based Network Intrusion Detection. This survey examines the use of deep reinforcement learning for network intrusion detection. It introduces approaches such as deep Q-networks and actor-critic methods, then reviews how they are applied to identifying malicious network activity. The discussion highlights practical challenges including training cost, class imbalance, rare and unknown attacks, feature selection, and deployment in Internet of Things environments. It also outlines research directions for more adaptive intrusion detection systems.

title: A Survey of Network-based Intrusion Detection Data Sets
document_text: A Survey of Network-based Intrusion Detection Data Sets. This paper reviews datasets used to train and evaluate anomaly-based network intrusion detection systems. It compares packet-based and flow-based data and proposes a structured set of properties for judging dataset suitability, including data volume and capture environment. The survey summarizes publicly available intrusion detection collections, explains differences between them, and discusses traffic generators and repositories that can support reproducible cybersecurity experiments.

title: Experimental Review of Neural-based approaches for Network Intrusion Management
document_text: Experimental Review of Neural-based approaches for Network Intrusion Management. This experimental review studies neural network approaches for managing network intrusions. It considers attacks that can evade traditional signature-based or deterministic rules, and compares deep learning and other neural techniques on newer network security datasets. The experiments examine both single-class and multi-class detection, accuracy, F-measure, and computational cost. The paper discusses trade-offs that security practitioners should consider when choosing neural intrusion detection models.

title: Unraveling the Key of Machine Learning Solutions for Android Malware Detection
document_text: Unraveling the Key of Machine Learning Solutions for Android Malware Detection. This study investigates machine learning methods for Android malware detection and organizes prior work according to feature engineering and model design. The authors reimplement representative approaches and compare effectiveness, robustness, and efficiency. The analysis emphasizes that stronger algorithms alone do not automatically produce better detectors; feature choices, evaluation conditions, and robustness also matter. The paper summarizes remaining challenges and offers recommendations for future Android application security research.

title: Android Malware Detection using Machine learning: A Review
document_text: Android Malware Detection using Machine learning: A Review. This review describes Android malware and the security risks malicious applications pose to mobile devices and user data. It surveys supervised learning, unsupervised learning, and deep learning methods used to identify malicious Android apps. It also compares evaluation practices and performance measures reported in the literature, discusses limitations of current detection techniques, and identifies directions for improving mobile malware analysis and classification.

title: Detection of Malicious Android Applications: Classical Machine Learning vs. Deep Neural Network Integrated with Clustering
document_text: Detection of Malicious Android Applications: Classical Machine Learning vs. Deep Neural Network Integrated with Clustering. This paper compares classical machine learning and deep neural approaches for detecting malicious Android applications. It studies feature reduction, classification, and clustering as parts of an Android malware detection pipeline. The experiments report that Random Forest performs strongly across several metrics, while clustering can further separate regions of the feature space. The work also considers how feature reduction affects computational efficiency and detection effectiveness.

title: Ransomware Detection and Classification using Machine Learning
document_text: Ransomware Detection and Classification using Machine Learning. This study focuses on identifying and classifying ransomware by analyzing behavioral characteristics and extracting features that distinguish ransomware families. It evaluates machine learning classifiers, particularly XGBoost and Random Forest, for recognizing ransomware activity. The paper frames early detection and classification as important cybersecurity tasks because ransomware can affect computers, servers, mobile applications, and web services. Its findings motivate the use of data-driven models in ransomware defense.

title: Can Features for Phishing URL Detection Be Trusted Across Diverse Datasets? A Case Study with Explainable AI
document_text: Can Features for Phishing URL Detection Be Trusted Across Diverse Datasets? A Case Study with Explainable AI. This work questions whether machine learning features for phishing URL detection generalize across datasets. It compares two public phishing URL collections whose URL-string and website-content indicators overlap only partially. The study tests cross-dataset model transfer and applies explainable AI methods such as SHAP to inspect feature contributions. Its central message is that apparently useful phishing indicators can depend on the dataset, so evaluation should test generalization rather than relying on one benchmark.

title: Network Security Modeling using NetFlow Data: Detecting Botnet attacks in IP Traffic
document_text: Network Security Modeling using NetFlow Data: Detecting Botnet attacks in IP Traffic. This research uses NetFlow records to detect botnet command-and-control hosts in large volumes of IP traffic. It performs exploratory analysis and derives network traffic features, then develops statistical and deep learning models for identifying malicious traces. Interpretable machine learning is used to characterize botnet traffic patterns. The reported predictions are checked against published malicious-IP blacklists, illustrating how flow telemetry can support network security monitoring.

title: AI-Driven Fast and Early Detection of IoT Botnet Threats: A Comprehensive Network Traffic Analysis Approach
document_text: AI-Driven Fast and Early Detection of IoT Botnet Threats: A Comprehensive Network Traffic Analysis Approach. This paper investigates early identification of Internet of Things botnets by analyzing network traffic, including packet-level and flow-level information. It considers stealthy command-and-control communication that can occur before a visible attack. The approach studies traffic features and semi-supervised learning on the IoT-23 dataset, which contains diverse botnet behaviors and attack scenarios. The work emphasizes timely bot detection, low false alarms, and practical network monitoring.

title: Advancing Email Spam Detection: Leveraging Zero-Shot Learning and Large Language Models
document_text: Advancing Email Spam Detection: Leveraging Zero-Shot Learning and Large Language Models. This study explores email spam classification with zero-shot learning and large language models. It combines language processing with a BERT-based component for extracting useful email information and a FLAN-T5 model for zero-shot classification. The motivation is to reduce dependence on large labeled datasets and frequent retraining as spam tactics change. The paper discusses adaptability to new spam patterns, class imbalance, data scarcity, and adversarial email content.

title: A Survey of Machine Learning Algorithms for Detecting Ransomware Encryption Activity
document_text: A Survey of Machine Learning Algorithms for Detecting Ransomware Encryption Activity. This survey reviews machine learning techniques for detecting ransomware encryption behavior using system-level measurements. It discusses telemetry such as processor clock speed, temperature, and CPU load as signals that may change during file encryption. The study compares classifiers including multilayer perceptrons and Random Forest, and considers accuracy, F1-score, and false-negative rate. It presents sensor-based monitoring as one possible way to identify suspicious encryption activity early.

title: Information Retrieval: Recent Advances and Beyond
document_text: Information Retrieval: Recent Advances and Beyond. This overview explains the main stages and model families used in modern information retrieval systems. It covers traditional term-based retrieval, semantic retrieval, and neural retrieval, and discusses how these approaches are trained and combined in search pipelines. The paper is intended as an introduction to current retrieval methods for researchers and practitioners. It provides context for comparing sparse keyword matching with learned representations of queries and documents.

title: Expand, Rerank, and Retrieve: Query Reranking for Open-Domain Question Answering
document_text: Expand, Rerank, and Retrieve: Query Reranking for Open-Domain Question Answering. This paper introduces an approach called EAR for improving passage retrieval in open-domain question answering. The method generates multiple expanded versions of an initial query and then reranks those queries to select expansions expected to retrieve useful passages. The approach connects query expansion with the behavior of the underlying retriever instead of selecting expansions only by generation probability. Experiments report improvements over a basic query expansion pipeline.

title: BERT-QE: Contextualized Query Expansion for Document Re-ranking
document_text: BERT-QE: Contextualized Query Expansion for Document Re-ranking. This work addresses vocabulary mismatch between a user query and relevant documents. It proposes BERT-QE, a contextualized query expansion method that selects useful document segments for adding expansion terms. The method aims to avoid irrelevant information that can be introduced by unconstrained query expansion. Experiments on established retrieval collections evaluate its effect on document reranking and compare it with contextual language model baselines.

title: Document Expansion by Query Prediction
document_text: Document Expansion by Query Prediction. This paper expands documents with terms predicted from the kinds of queries users might submit. A sequence-to-sequence model learns to generate likely queries for a document from query-document training pairs, and the predicted terms are added to the document representation. The purpose is to reduce mismatch between the wording of a document and the wording of a search query. The method is evaluated with a reranking component for retrieval tasks.

title: ColBERT: Efficient and Effective Passage Search via Contextualized Late Interaction over BERT
document_text: ColBERT: Efficient and Effective Passage Search via Contextualized Late Interaction over BERT. ColBERT is a neural retrieval model that independently encodes queries and documents with BERT and compares their token representations using a late-interaction operation. Separating encoding from interaction allows document representations to be computed in advance while retaining fine-grained query-document matching. The design aims to balance the contextual understanding of large language models with efficient passage search. The paper evaluates retrieval effectiveness and computational cost on passage-search datasets.

title: Unsupervised Dense Information Retrieval with Contrastive Learning
document_text: Unsupervised Dense Information Retrieval with Contrastive Learning. This study investigates dense information retrieval when labeled query-document pairs are unavailable. It trains neural retrievers with unsupervised contrastive learning and evaluates them on the BEIR benchmark. The results show that contrastive pretraining can provide competitive retrieval quality and can be used before supervised fine-tuning. The paper also explores multilingual retrieval and cross-lingual transfer, highlighting the potential of dense representations in settings with limited relevance labels.

title: InPars: Data Augmentation for Information Retrieval using Large Language Models
document_text: InPars: Data Augmentation for Information Retrieval using Large Language Models. InPars uses large language models to generate synthetic query and passage training examples for information retrieval. The motivation is that a single general-purpose relevance dataset may not fit every retrieval domain. The generated examples provide domain-oriented supervision for training neural retrievers, even when manually labeled relevance data is scarce. The paper evaluates retrievers trained with synthetic data against traditional and self-supervised baselines and studies transfer to other retrieval tasks.

title: SPLADE: Sparse Lexical and Expansion Model for First Stage Ranking
document_text: SPLADE: Sparse Lexical and Expansion Model for First Stage Ranking. SPLADE is a neural sparse retrieval model designed for the first stage of search ranking. It learns sparse term-weight representations for queries and documents, combining lexical matching with expansion to related terms. Its sparse vectors retain advantages associated with bag-of-words retrieval, including explicit terms and compatibility with inverted indexes, while learning richer term weights. The work studies the trade-off between retrieval effectiveness and efficiency.

title: Approximate Nearest Neighbor Negative Contrastive Learning for Dense Text Retrieval
document_text: Approximate Nearest Neighbor Negative Contrastive Learning for Dense Text Retrieval. This paper proposes ANCE, a training method for dense text retrieval. It identifies a mismatch between easy negative examples used during training and the difficult irrelevant documents encountered at search time. ANCE uses an approximate nearest-neighbor index of the corpus to mine more realistic negative passages while training. The approach updates this index during learning and aims to improve dense ranking quality while keeping retrieval practical at scale.

title: Query Expansion Using Contextual Clue Sampling with Language Models
document_text: Query Expansion Using Contextual Clue Sampling with Language Models. This work studies query expansion with contexts generated by language models. It argues that expansion terms should be both diverse and relevant: sampling multiple contexts can increase diversity but may also introduce hallucinated or unrelated information. The proposed method filters generated contexts and combines retrieved documents according to context-generation probabilities. Its lexical retrieval approach is evaluated against dense retrieval baselines and considers index-size efficiency.

title: Precise Zero-Shot Dense Retrieval without Relevance Labels
document_text: Precise Zero-Shot Dense Retrieval without Relevance Labels. This paper proposes Hypothetical Document Embeddings, or HyDE, for dense retrieval without labeled relevance data. Given a query, a language model first writes a hypothetical document that represents a possible relevant answer. An unsupervised encoder then embeds that generated text and uses the vector to find nearby real documents in the corpus. The approach uses the language model to bridge query-document vocabulary differences while grounding final results in actual indexed documents.

title: Learning to Retrieve Passages without Supervision
document_text: Learning to Retrieve Passages without Supervision. This research explores unsupervised pretraining for passage retrieval in open-domain question answering. Its recurring-span retrieval method creates pseudo query-passage examples from spans that appear across passages in a document, supporting contrastive learning without manually labeled queries. The method aims to capture both lexical overlap and semantic relations. Experiments report zero-shot retrieval performance and examine combining the learned dense retriever with a sparse BM25 system.

title: Promptagator: Few-shot Dense Retrieval From 8 Examples
document_text: Promptagator: Few-shot Dense Retrieval From 8 Examples. Promptagator studies dense retrieval in task-specific settings where only a small number of examples are available. It uses a language model to generate synthetic queries from a short task description and a few examples, then trains a retriever on the generated data. The work argues that retrieval tasks have different intents and domains, so task-specific data generation can be useful. It evaluates the approach across multiple retrieval collections.

title: RocketQA: An Optimized Training Approach to Dense Passage Retrieval for Open-Domain Question Answering
document_text: RocketQA: An Optimized Training Approach to Dense Passage Retrieval for Open-Domain Question Answering. RocketQA is an optimized training framework for dense passage retrieval in open-domain question answering. It addresses training difficulties such as limited labeled examples, unlabeled relevant passages, and the difference between training and inference. Its components include cross-batch negatives, denoised hard negatives, and data augmentation. The paper evaluates the framework on passage retrieval benchmarks and studies how better retrieval can improve downstream question answering.

title: Text Embeddings by Weakly-Supervised Contrastive Pre-training
document_text: Text Embeddings by Weakly-Supervised Contrastive Pre-training. This paper presents E5, a family of general-purpose text embedding models trained with weakly supervised contrastive learning. The training data consists of large collections of text pairs, and the resulting embeddings are evaluated on retrieval, clustering, and classification tasks. The work reports strong zero-shot and fine-tuned results across BEIR and MTEB datasets. It illustrates how a shared vector representation can support several language processing and search applications.

title: SimCSE: Simple Contrastive Learning of Sentence Embeddings
document_text: SimCSE: Simple Contrastive Learning of Sentence Embeddings. SimCSE is a contrastive learning framework for producing sentence embeddings. Its unsupervised version uses dropout as a minimal source of augmentation by comparing different representations of the same sentence. A supervised variant uses entailment pairs as positive examples and contradiction pairs as hard negatives. The paper evaluates sentence representations on semantic textual similarity tasks and discusses how contrastive objectives improve alignment between related sentences.

title: Towards General Text Embeddings with Multi-stage Contrastive Learning
document_text: Towards General Text Embeddings with Multi-stage Contrastive Learning. This work introduces GTE, a general-purpose text embedding model trained through multiple stages of contrastive learning. It combines diverse datasets during unsupervised pretraining and supervised fine-tuning to improve representations across tasks. The model is evaluated on text embedding benchmarks and code retrieval settings. The paper presents multi-stage contrastive training as a way to build reusable embeddings for semantic search, ranking, and other language applications.

title: MTEB: Massive Text Embedding Benchmark
document_text: MTEB: Massive Text Embedding Benchmark. MTEB is a benchmark created to evaluate text embedding models across a broad range of tasks rather than relying on semantic similarity alone. It covers retrieval, reranking, clustering, classification, and other embedding applications across many datasets and languages. By evaluating numerous models under a shared framework, the study shows that no single embedding method dominates every task. The benchmark helps researchers compare embedding quality more comprehensively.
